       COLORADO RIVER ALLIANCE INTERVENORS’ REPLY TO EXCEPTIONS

 TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES AND COMMISSIONERS:

         Brushy Mountain Road Maintenance Association, Inc.; Rio Agua Investments,

 LLC; KDCB Garrett Ranch LTD; SSS Land Holdings, LLC; and BTR Burnet LP

 (together, the “Colorado River Alliance Intervenors” or “CRAI”) file this Reply to

 Exceptions certain intervenors filed pursuant to the Exceptions and Replies

 memorandum dated August 20, 2026, and respectfully show the following:

 I.      INTRODUCTION AND SUMMARY.

         Most intervenors’ exceptions support denial of the Application, as the Proposal

 for Decision (“PFD”) recommends;1 some of these intervenors also object to the

 recommendation of Route 894 as the route to be selected, if the Application is not




 1      See, e.g., G-9 and G-13 Landowners’ Exceptions to Proposal for Decision at 2; 4K Land
 and Cattle Company’s Exceptions to Proposal for Decision at 2; Save the Lampasas’
 Exceptions to the Alternative Recommendation in the Proposal for Decision at 1-2.

 PUC Docket No. 59475                                                               Page 1
 Colorado River Alliance Intervenors’ Reply to Exceptions
 denied.2 The Applicants except to the proposal for decision’s determination that notice

was improper and that the Applicants failed to prove that the transmission line made the

basis of their Application is necessary.3

        CRAI supports the PFD, both with respect to its findings on notice, its

determination that the proposed transmission line is not necessary, and its

determination that if a route is to be selected, it should be Route 894. Apart from the

PFD’s determinations on notice and necessity, most parties filing exceptions focus on

the same routing issues argued in their initial and reply post-hearing briefs, essentially

complaining about either the weighting of the evidence or the Administrative Law

Judges’ (“ALJs’”) explanation of the proposed decision. CRAI does not object to certain

routes excepting parties advocate, as those routes conform to Commission-selection

criteria as well, or nearly as well, as Route 894—including Route 392 and particularly

Route 410. CRAI responds to the arguments of excepting parties as follows.

        Under PUC PROC. R. § 22.262(a):

        The commission may change a finding of fact or conclusion of law made by the
        administrative law judge[s] . . . only if the commission . . . determines that the
        administrative law judge[s] [either] . . . did not properly apply or interpret
        applicable law, commission rules or policies, or prior administrative decisions; or .
        . . issued a finding of fact that is not supported by a preponderance of the
        evidence . . . or determines that . . . a prior administrative decision on which the
        administrative law judge[s] relied is incorrect or should be changed.

Here the parties excepting to the PFD failed to demonstrate that the findings in the PFD

are inadequately supported or that the ALJs failed to faithfully apply PURA § 37.056 or

PUC SUBST. R. § 25.101(b)(3)(B). The PFD should be adopted in its entirety.


2      See, e.g., 4K Land and Cattle Company’s Exceptions to Proposal for Decision at 2; Save
the Lampasas’ Exceptions to the Alternative Recommendation in the Proposal for Decision at 2.
3       Applicants’ Exceptions to the Proposal for Decision at 10-41, 41-76.

Colorado River Alliance Intervenors’ Reply to Exceptions
 II.     REPLY ARGUMENTS.

        E.      Route

                8.      Weighing the Factors in PURA § 37.056(c) and PUC Subst. R. §
                        25.101(b)(3)(B), which proposed transmission-line route is the
                        best alternative?

        The record makes clear that, if a route is to be selected, Route 894 is the route

that best meets the requirements of PURA § 37.056(c) and PUC SUBST. R. §

25.101(b)(3)(B), followed closely by Routes 392 and 410.




       Figure 1.       Reformatted excerpt from Oncor & LCRA TSC Ex. 23, Combined Data
                       Tables, for routes of interest.




PUC Docket No. 59475                                                            Page 3
Colorado River Alliance Intervenors’ Reply to Exceptions
         a.       Direct comparisons of primary routes in contention.

        Like the other recent 765-kV transmission line routing disputes, beyond the

question of procedural irregularities or the Applicants’ failure to prove that the Project is

necessary, as required in PURA, a common theme may be found throughout the

exceptions: Either the PFD got it right in endorsing Route 894 or got it wrong, and other

routes—routes that do not negatively affect the proponent—better meet the

Commission’s criteria. When Route 894 is compared against alternative routes

intervenors impacted by Route 894 support, a balanced analysis of the data in the

record confirms Route 894 is the route the Commission should approve, if it approves a

route at all. The following summarizes the attributes of the routes those impacted by

Route 894 urge:

                Route 296. The few parties who champion Route 296 emphasize that it
                 parallels more combined compatible rights-of-way and property
                 boundaries than Route 894 (47.07% vs. 43.92%). But as the Combined
                 Data Tables establish, that is the only primary data point in Route 296’s
                 favor.4 Both the quantitative and qualitative metrics belie any claim that
                 Route 296 is superior.

                    o Route 894 is less costly.

                    o Route 894 directly affects 20 fewer habitable structures within 500
                      feet of the centerline.

                    o More importantly, Route 894 does not impact any elementary
                      schools or churches among its 85 habitable structures.5


4         Oncor & LCRA TSC Ex. 23, Combined Data Tables (derived of Oncor & LCRA TSC Exs.
1 and 1A, Application and Errata, Tables 7-1 (Route Composition), 7-2 (Environmental Data),
Attachment 4 (Estimated Costs)). Route 296 is longer, is more costly, affects more habitable
structures (including two churches and a Florence ISD elementary school), has more park
visibility, crosses far more streams, and more, than Route 894. Id.
5      Route 296, comprised in part of Link F34, does, in fact, directly impact both a Florence
ISD elementary school and two churches among its 105 recorded habitable structures. See
FISD Exhibit 1 (Direct Testimony); Oncor & LCRA TSC Ex. 1A (Errata); Oncor & LCRA TSC Ex.
23 (Combined Data Tables).

PUC Docket No. 59475                                                                 Page 4
Colorado River Alliance Intervenors’ Reply to Exceptions
                     o Route 894 crosses fewer streams.

                    o Route 894 has no estimated length of right-of-way within the
                      foreground visual zone of park/recreational areas.

                    o Route 894 crosses fewer cultural resource sites.

                    o Route 894 does not cross scientifically identified golden-cheeked
                      warbler habitat6 or a habitat mitigation bank, while Route 296 does
                      intrude on those preserved habitats.7

               Route 392. Route 392 is demonstrably better than Route 296 and is
                qualitatively comparable in many ways to Route 894.

                    o Route 894 is marginally less costly than Route 392 and affects
                      fewer habitable structures.

                    o Of those opposing Route 894, their primary complaint is that it
                      crosses the Colorado River at an undeveloped area that is
                      otherwise unremarkable.8 But Route 392 crosses the Colorado
                      River at a point where an existing transmission line crosses the
                      river.

                    o Route 392 does an excellent job of minimizing the impacts on
                      landowners by paralleling almost 24 miles of existing transmission
                      line and more than 17 miles of public roads and highways. Route
                      894 does comparatively poorly on this criterion, and Route 296
                      parallels substantially less than Route 392.9

                    o Route 392 crosses more streams and recorded cultural resources
                      and is near substantially more areas of high potential.

               Route 410. Generally, the parties that favor Route 392 also support Route
                410. By contrast to Route 296, Route 410 affects only 98 habitable
                structures—and does so without utilizing Link F34, with its attendant
                impacts on Florence Elementary School and two churches. The Combined
                Data Tables10 and the remainder of the record demonstrate that Route

warblers in the path of Link J31).
7      See Underwood Ex. 34 (Blair Direct) (“Segment J31 appears that it would cross directly
through land designated as Golden-Cheeked Warbler mitigation acreage.”)
8       Solana Intervenors’ Exceptions to the Proposal for Decision at 26-29.

                 410 offers some quantitative advantages over Route 894 and numerous
                advantages over Route 296.

                    o Route 894 is ten miles shorter and somewhat less costly than
                      Route 410, directly affects fewer habitable structures within 500
                      feet of the centerline, crosses fewer streams, crosses fewer cultural
                      resource sites, and crosses fewer miles of potential areas of high
                      archeological and historical sites.

                    o Route 410 provides, however, substantially better paralleling—and
                      substantially better paralleling than Route 296—including
                      paralleling an existing transmission line across the Colorado River
                      on Link U3.11

                    o Neither Route 894 nor Route 410 crosses scientifically identified
                      golden-cheeked warbler habitat or a habitat mitigation bank at Link
                      J31.12

               Route “CCG” or “Cherokee G”.13 Like other routes examined in
                exceptions, Route CCG also does not utilize Link F34, but the Combined
                Data Tables and the record highlight that Route CCG pales in comparison
                to Route 894.

                    o Route 894 is substantially less costly (almost $74,000,000);
                      moreover, Route CCG is the highest cost route anyone proposes to
                      be adopted.14



11      See Hodge/Schwertner Ex. 1, Ex. BCA-3.
12      See fn. 7, 8.
13      According to one expert, Route CCG—a so-called “RFI route”—is necessarily “biased” in
its design to avoid the impacted intervenors who proposed it; Route CCG was not described in
the Application. 5TR 269:19-270:12 (Anderson)(RFI routes “all reflect the bias of their single
sole expert or the landowner themselves”). Importantly, the Joint Applicants provided no notice
of Route CCG (or “Cherokee G” in the Colorado River Alliance Intervenors’ Initial Brief) pursuant
to PUC PROC. R. § 22.52. See 3TR. 47:19-24, 49:15-18 (Perkins) (“Q. . . . I’m just asking you
whether you sent out PUC Rule 22.52 notice to persons affected by the RFI routes after they
were devised? A. (Perkins) Not after they were devised.”). As such, the limited availability of
cross-examination unduly affected parties’ ability to test Route CCG at the hearing on the
merits, implicating a lack of due process.
14       Importantly, Cherokee Creek Aligned Intervenor witness Reinecke completely disregards
cost in making her recommendation of Route CCG. CCG Ex. 1 (Reinecke Dir.)(mentioning the
cost factor in the framework, but expressly declining to address it in any way). While cost is not
the only—or often, even the primary—factor driving a routing decision, here, the difference in
costs between Route 894 and Route CCG is substantial. Yet Reinecke disregarded it
explicitly. CCP Ex. 2 28:13-18 (Reinecke Cross-reb.).

PUC Docket No. 59475                                                                    Page 6
Colorado River Alliance Intervenors’ Reply to Exceptions
                     o Route 894 is almost 10 miles shorter that Route CCG, which is the
                      second longest route described in exceptions.

                    o Route CCG directly affects more habitable structures within 500
                      feet of the centerline than any route described in exceptions, except
                      Route 392. Route CCG directly affects more habitable structures
                      than Route 894, Route 410, or Route 487.

                    o Route 894 crosses significantly fewer streams than Route CCG,
                      which crosses substantially more streams than any of the routes
                      discussed in exceptions.

                    o Route 894 not only crosses fewer cultural resource sites than
                      Route CCG, but it also crosses almost eight fewer miles of potential
                      areas of high archeological and historical sites.

                    o Route 894 does not cross scientifically-identified golden-cheeked
                      warbler habitat or a habitat mitigation bank, while Route CCG
                      does.15

At bottom, while the Commission could reasonably select either Route 392 or Route

410 for their better paralleling and Colorado River crossing—and their attendant

“moderat[ion of] impact[s] on the affected community and landowners,” PUC SUBST. R. §

25.101(b)(3)(B) requires—on balance, Route 894 best satisfies the criteria the

Commission is to consider in routing a transmission line.




15     The only “observations” of impacts on golden-cheeked warbler habitat made the basis of
Cherokee Creek, et al.’s, Save the Lampasas’s, and other testimony are theoretical, anecdotal,
or unsupported by scientific studies, other than those described in the Environmental
Assessment, which confirms that the contractors did no independent, onsite work—and made
no independent observations. This contrasts to the evidence of two expert witnesses to the
impact of a route utilizing Link J31, such as Route 296 or Route CCG, upon a studied
population and habitat mitigation bank. See Ex. CRAI-5 (Morrison Dir.)(J31 impacts habitat and
studied population of golden-cheeked warblers); Underwood Ex. 34 (Blair Dir.)(J31 impacts
golden-cheeked warbler mitigation bank).

PUC Docket No. 59475                                                                Page 7
Colorado River Alliance Intervenors’ Reply to Exceptions
         b.      Comparisons of discussions reveal biases, not reasons to choose
                other routes.

                i.      Proponents of Route 296 merely avoid themselves and their
                        allies; they do not provide substantial support for its selection.

        As set forth above, Route 296 pales in comparison to Routes 894, 392, and 410,

among others, because it unduly affects community values, is longer, is more costly,

and does not present the best Colorado River crossing—or even the second best. Filing

three briefs for clients with disparate interests that say essentially the same thing, “Save

the Lampasas,” N3, and Carpenter (collectively, the “STL Parties”), attempt to amplify

their arguments through repetitious filings, never confiding that their combined group

has had to solve a puzzle not on the merits, but on reconciling disparate group interests

spanning more than one-third of the study area.16 Then, the STL Parties aggregate their

multitudinous differential attributes and interests into a coordinated, but flawed,

“community” of support for Route 296.17

        No doubt, each route in the Application or proposed in Requests for Information

imposes individualized impacts on each directly affected landowner, including the STL



16      There are multiple ways of measuring the geographic disparity of interests that resulted
in only Route 296 satisfying all of them, but some members of the STL Parties are almost 125
miles apart, and the total geographic area over which the STL Parties are spread is
approximately one-third of the Study Area.
17      See Exceptions filed by the STL Parties. The parties represented by STL are located
somewhere proximate to the Lampasas River or one of its tributaries and affected by Link G51;
N3, located more than 100 miles west of the Lampasas River and affected by Link N3; and
Carpenter, located more than 20 miles to the west of the Lampasas River and affected by Link
J22. These intervenors may certainly team up and decide not to advocate for routes that affect
any of their disparate groups adversely, but they may not legitimately claim that they have a
common set of “community values,” because theirs are separate communities the only common
interest of which is the avoidance of the line and foisting it upon other landowners. Their
advocacy of Route 296, which has few redeeming characteristics—and many flaws, including
routing near the Florence Elementary School and two churches—is outclassed not only by
Route 894, but also Route 392 and Route 410.

PUC Docket No. 59475                                                                  Page 8
Colorado River Alliance Intervenors’ Reply to Exceptions
 Parties. On balance, however, the facts support the PFD’s recommendation of Route

894.

                A)      The Colorado River crossing on Route 296, Link J31, is
                        problematic.

        Parties attempting to push the Commission’s routing decision south, incorrectly

characterize previous PUC decisions on crossings of the Colorado River. While the STL

Parties claim that there was some sort of approval of a crossing in the vicinity of what is

now Link J31, in fact (1) the entire application in issue in Docket No. 37448 was

rejected—including specifically a route using a Colorado River crossing near the

location of J31; (2) the crossing at Link J31 has substantial negative attributes that are

described in both Docket No. 37448 and in the record in this docket. At bottom, nothing

“positive” about a Link J31 crossing overcomes the substantial negative attributes of

Route 296. Link G51 itself, about which most of STL Parties’ contentions of harm arise,

is no closer than four miles from the Lampasas River itself. Importantly, the STL Parties’

contentions about Docket No. 37448 are undermined by a simple comparison of

maps—Ex. BCI 62 overlays the two maps, showing clearly that the crossings the

Commission rejected were similar to Link J26 and Link J31, not Link J22, a component

of Route 894.




PUC Docket No. 59475                                                             Page 9
Colorado River Alliance Intervenors’ Reply to Exceptions
         Figure 2.       Excerpt from Exhibit BCI 62 reflecting paths of Links J26, J22, and
                        J31 in comparison to Docket No. 37448 Links C20 and C22 across
                        the Colorado River.18


        Isolated from all other factors that must be balanced under Commission criteria,

there is little question but that the “best” Colorado River crossing is at Link U3, where

that segment parallels an existing transmission line as it crosses the river. Other factors,

beyond the benefits of a Link U3 crossing, support Route 392 and Route 410, but the

advantage of utilizing a Link U3 crossing is substantial.



18     See Ex. CRAI-11 (depicting relative positions of Links J22, J26, and J31 as they cross
the Colorado River); see also id. Ex. BCI 62. For Smitherman confirming that it looks accurate
5TR. 187:6 (Smitherman).


PUC Docket No. 59475                                                                  Page 10
Colorado River Alliance Intervenors’ Reply to Exceptions
                 B)      The theorized “minor modification” of Link F34 to “improve”
                        Route 296 is a costly, unattainable distraction.

        Route 296 requires the use of Link F34; Link F34 unduly impacts both the

Florence Elementary School and at least two churches—obstacles to approval that

were not identified in the Application. In an attempt to bolster their support of Route 296,

their triangulated route, the STL Parties argue that a non-consensual “minor

modification” on a non-party’s land could be devised that would mitigate the impact to

the Florence Elementary.19 G-9 and G-13 Landowners and Yates echo the “downside”

that could be “mitigated.”20 But at least three problems arise:

        (1)     No consent to the rerouting has been obtained from the noticed, but

                unconsulted, landowner that would be affected by the hypothetical

                modification;

        (2)     The rerouting would bisect the tract on which the STL Parties contemplate

                the revision, not paralleling closely that property’s boundaries; and

        (3)     The STL Parties’ geometry (and cost-math) is lacking: the rerouting makes

                an already more expensive Route 296 still more so by adding not one, but




19      STL Exceptions at 9.
20      G-9 G-13 Landowners Exceptions at 6; Yates Exceptions at 14.

PUC Docket No. 59475                                                                Page 11
Colorado River Alliance Intervenors’ Reply to Exceptions
                 two dead-end structures to Route 296.21

Beyond the Florence Elementary School and church impacts shown to accompany

Route 296, the record also reflects that Link F34 will be substantially impacted by a

planned highway interchange that further complicates the use of Route 296.22 While no

one factor is dispositive, the nature of the impacts of Route 296 on the affected

communities, particularly those proximate to its component Link F34, is substantial.

                C)      Proponents of Route 296 claim unsubstantiated ecological
                        benefits.

        While the STL Parties talk about “documented” (i.e., anecdotally seen or

modeled) golden-cheeked warbler habitat, they ignore (1) evidence that routes using

Link J31 cut through scientifically studied and documented golden-cheeked warbler

habitat occupied with warblers;23 and (2) uncontradicted testimony that Link J31 would

 cross through an existing golden-cheeked warbler habitat mitigation bank.24 All other

would fragment the documented habitat and that the “existing infrastructure,” a pipeline

                D)      Proponents of Route 296 favor the protection of their own
                        ranches over those of their neighbors.

        Bisection of properties should be avoided, and the routes in this docket—as all

recent dockets—do a poor job of identifying actual property boundaries, much less

paralleling them. But N3 elevates its parochial interests in avoiding its members over

the real, documented issues.25 For instance, N3 discounts the Route 296 bisection of

the historic Taylor-Rose Ranch, being comprised in its entirely by a Texas Historical

Commission Trinomial.26 In passing, N3 contends without citation that the negatives

associated with Route 296, including its undue proximity to Florence Elementary School

and two churches, may be “easily mitigated.”27

        Nothing about Route 296 elevates it over the alternatives.

                 ii.     Proponents of Route 392 and Route 410 make a better case
                        that northern alternatives—particularly those that cross the
                        Colorado River in parallel to an existing transmission line on
                        Link U3—are superior in many ways to Route 296.

        Several parties make reasonable arguments for alternative routes in the northern

corridor. For instance 4K contends that, among others, Route 410 is superior.28 4K also

contends that Route 894 passes through golden-cheeked warbler habitat, but relies

upon anecdotal testimony, not scientific surveys, in support.29 In fact, the only

established, occupied golden-cheeked warbler habitat and mitigation bank are located

on Link J31.

        4K correctly reiterates the paralleling advantages of Routes 392 and 410—hard,

existing infrastructure, including existing transmission lines and roadways—particularly

proximate to the Link U3 Colorado River crossing. 30

        Likewise, the Brady Creek Intervenors propose that the Commission select

Route 392 or Route 410 in lieu of Route 894.31 While CRAI contends that Route 894 is,

in fact, statistically superior to the alternatives, the northern routes also have

advantages:

        (A)     They generally parallel existing infrastructure, roads and transmission

                lines, better.

        (B)     They affect only marginally higher numbers of habitable structures.

        (C)     They are only marginally higher in cost.

28      4K Exceptions at 7. 4K also contends that Routes 416 and 392 rank highly under its
multi-factor analysis. Id. at 9-10.
29      Id. at 19-20.

31      BCI Exceptions at 1-2.

PUC Docket No. 59475                                                                 Page 14
Colorado River Alliance Intervenors’ Reply to Exceptions
         (D)     They cross the Colorado River at the most advantageous location, Link

                U3, paralleling existing transmission line infrastructure.

        On prudent avoidance, the increased structure counts in the northern corridor are

overcome by the relatively small number of structures per route mile32 and, more

importantly—these northern corridor routes parallel far more existing infrastructure and

cross the Colorado River while paralleling such infrastructure than many routes.33

                iii.    Cherokee Creek’s contentions in favor of Route CCG are
                        belied by the facts

        Because the numbers generally speak for themselves, the opponents of Route

894 are left to overstate certain qualitative reasons to avoid links on Route 894 or to use

certain links on other alternative routes. Alleged potential impacts upon Ecologically

Significant Stream Segments (“ESSS”) is one example. As Cherokee Creek Aligned

Intervenors persist in contending in their exceptions, “Route 894 crosses the ESSS

portion of the Colorado River.”34 However, that group’s own expert, Ms. Reinecke,

testified to the contrary and acknowledged that Route 894 also avoids the ESSS portion

of the Colorado River.35 In the same vein, the Cherokee Creek group also argued that

its preferred Route CCG “avoids USFWS Karst Zone 1 and the Edwards Aquifer

 altogether.”36 But just like its ESSS claim, Cherokee Creek’s expert was forced to

concede that Route 894 also avoids both the Karst Zone and Edwards Aquifer.37

        Nothing about Route CCG elevates it above the route recommended in the PFD,

Route 894.

III.    CONCLUSION.

        For all of the reasons proven in the record, the Colorado River Alliance

Intervenors respectfully request that the Commission adopt the PFD, reject the

Application, or in the alternative, select Route 894.
